overview: This record follows modern Iraq, whose monarchy ended in 1958 and whose Ba’ath government emerged a decade later. It does not combine the ancient Mesopotamian kingdoms or Abbasid Caliphate into one uninterrupted state. The imported span begins in 1945; five broad outlines run only to 2020. They do not show changing wartime control or internal regional government, and their last year is not Iraq’s disappearance.

periods.title: The monarchy
periods.summary: An independent kingdom continued until the July 1958 coup ended the monarchy.

periods.title: Early republican governments
periods.summary: The monarchy’s overthrow established a republic, followed by further political changes.

periods.title: Ba’ath rule
periods.summary: The Ba’ath Party held power; Saddam Hussein became president in 1979.

periods.title: Invasion and transition
periods.summary: The invasion removed the old regime; occupation authorities transferred power to an interim government in 2004.

periods.title: Federal constitutional republic
periods.summary: The constitution recognizes federal institutions, the Kurdistan region and multiple languages.

items.text: Iraq’s British mandate status ended in 1932, before this map record begins. A monarchy remained until the coup in Baghdad on 14 July 1958. That upheaval also ended Iraq’s short-lived union with Jordan. The political institution changed sharply, while cities, families and working communities continued through the transition.

The Ba’ath Party seized power in 1968. Saddam Hussein became president in 1979, concentrating authority at the top of the state. Iraq fought Iran from 1980 to 1988, while military production expanded. A country with major industrial ambitions also committed enormous resources to a prolonged and destructive war.

In the 1988 Anfal campaign, Saddam Hussein’s government attacked Kurdish communities, destroyed villages and made civilians disappear into detention and killing operations. Human Rights Watch reconstructed the campaign from captured government documents and interviews with survivors. This was organized persecution, not a natural disappearance of villages or a change that can be explained by a map colour.

Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990 brought international sanctions and the 1991 Gulf War. Ordinary households faced severe shortages and damaged services. The United Nations created Oil-for-Food in 1995, allowing supervised oil sales to finance food, medicine and other humanitarian needs. It was an emergency arrangement within sanctions, rather than ordinary unrestricted trade.

A coalition led by the United States and Britain invaded Iraq in March 2003 and captured Baghdad in April. Saddam’s government fell, and the Coalition Provisional Authority administered the occupation. Power passed to an Iraqi interim government in June 2004 amid insurgency and civil unrest. Removing the regime did not end the violence or erase the Iraqi state.

Baghdad hosted the conference that founded OPEC in September 1960. Iraq joined Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela as the five original members. Their representatives met in Al-Shaab Hall to coordinate oil-producing countries’ interests. Decisions made around a conference table connected Iraqi resources with the wider world’s demand for fuel.

The 2005 constitution describes Iraq as a federal parliamentary republic. It recognizes Arabic and Kurdish as official languages and the Kurdistan region as a federal region. These provisions acknowledge a country containing different communities and institutions. Constitutional promises describe the intended legal order; they do not by themselves prove equal treatment in everyday life.

sections.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills

items.text: In the southern marshes, a mudhif is a large gathering building made from reeds and papyrus. Bundles form sweeping arches, and woven mats furnish the interior. Skilled builders lead the work, but neighbours help collect materials and maintain the space. A community building can begin with plants gathered from the landscape around it.

A mudhif welcomes visitors and provides space for weddings, storytelling, discussion and the settlement of disagreements. Children and young people learn customs and craft skills through participation. UNESCO describes management by tribal sheikhs alongside community involvement. The same room may host serious conversation one day and a celebration the next.

Iraqi maqam brings Arabic poetry together with a singer and instrumental ensemble. The singer improvises while instruments such as the santur, jawzah fiddle and hand drums accompany the performance. UNESCO records gatherings in homes, coffeehouses and theatres. Listening is a social occasion as well as a musical one, with room for an experienced singer to surprise the audience.

Older Iraqi houses can have shanasheel, projecting windows with carved wooden latticework. A UNESCO architectural account explains how these features admit moving air while reducing direct sunlight. This is an inherited building tradition shared with neighbouring regions, not something invented by the modern state. A handsome window can also be hard-working shade.

In a 2021 FAO interview, Nineveh dairy farmer Dhuhaa Najm Shith recalled feeding her buffalo and milking them before sunrise. Her household sold raw milk and made qimar, a thick cream, for city markets. Work at home connected animal care, food processing and family income. Preparing breakfast ingredients could begin while customers were still asleep.

Marshland food production depends on sufficient water for people, reeds and buffalo. During a July 2022 visit, FAO reported low water, poor animal health and declining milk production. Some families were moving their herds to other places with water. This dated account shows why the future of a familiar food can depend on river management and climate.

At Mujahid al-Arabi Primary School in al-Karma, Anbar, children had studied in crowded temporary rooms after wartime damage. A 2023 UNDP account describes the rebuilt school’s library, clean toilets and drinking water, alongside football and friendships. Twelve-year-old Saif especially enjoyed maths. Rebuilding a school meant restoring ordinary routines as well as walls.

ISIL occupied Mosul in 2014 and destroyed al-Nouri Mosque during its retreat in 2017. Restoration teams first removed explosives and hazardous material, then sorted rubble for fragments that could be reused. Iraqi heritage specialists and international partners worked together. Rebuilding required patient recording and conservation, not simply clearing everything away and starting over.

Excavations near al-Nouri’s prayer hall began in August 2021 and uncovered four rooms dating to the twelfth century. Coins of the Atabeg period helped date them; jars, pottery and carved stone also appeared. Archaeologists think the rooms were probably used for ritual washing. The modern rebuilding project unexpectedly opened a window into an older building’s daily use.

Two children in Baghdad developed paralytic polio in 2014 after a long absence of the disease. Iraqi health authorities, WHO, UNICEF and other partners responded with vaccination campaigns coordinated across the region. WHO’s account describes transmission being interrupted within ten months. The achievement depended on reaching children repeatedly, including families displaced by conflict.

Floods in November 2018 damaged toilets, showers and water supplies in Jeddah and Airstrip camps near Qayyarah. UNICEF’s report describes workers clearing waste from sanitation systems while others restored drinking water and delivered soap and hygiene supplies. For displaced families, a working toilet also depended on drains, maintenance and safe water beyond the cubicle.

A 2015 WHO report describes a health clinic assembled from six caravans in a displaced-person camp on the Najaf road in Kerbala. It included a laboratory, pharmacy, wound-dressing rooms and maternal and child health services. Movable buildings brought several kinds of care together while families were living away from home.

Article 11 of the 2005 constitution reads “بغداد عاصمة جمهورية العراق”: “Baghdad is the capital of the Republic of Iraq.” A Latin transliteration is “Baghdād ʿāṣimat Jumhūriyyat al-ʿIrāq.” The Arabic sample comes from Parliament’s modern digital text, checked against the English constitutional translation. It is one official language’s writing, not a claim that every Iraqi speaks Arabic.

ending.text: Iraq continues as a state with federal constitutional institutions. The monarchy ended in 1958 and Ba’ath rule ended in 2003; neither event meant that Iraq’s peoples and communities disappeared. The dataset’s last polygon ends in 2020, but this is a limit of the imported maps, not a historical fall date.
